blocks.text: Now, to state modestly but freely what I find lacking in each: first, I would have this held as certain, that קפוד kippod and קפוז kippoz, however similar in sound, are nevertheless names of different animals. 1. Because in the same sequence of the text they are presented by Isaiah as different. The pelican, he says, and the KIPPOD shall possess it. And, a few words later, There shall the KIPPOZ make its nest. This is an empty repetition if kippod and kippoz were the same ^{(1)}. 2. Above all this: whereas I have proved in its place ^{a)} that קפוד kippod is the hedgehog, that is, a viviparous quadruped, קפוז kippoz, on the contrary, is described as an oviparous animal ^{(2)}: There shall the kippoz make its nest, and lay, and hatch (the eggs, that is), after it has (them) warmed in its shadow. What could be more explicit? Thus Santes and Schindlerus in their Lexicons, under the word בקע, seem plainly not to have known what kind of animal the hedgehog is; otherwise they would never have said, as they do in expounding this passage, that the hedgehog builds a nest, and breaks its eggs, and, when they are broken, hatches its young. [III, 196] Secondly, whatever קפוז kippoz may be, since it takes its name from leaping, it is neither the tortoise nor the bird cypselus. For leaping suits neither. Not the tortoise, which does not even walk except by crawling. Nor the bird cypselus, which others call apus, because it lacks the use of its feet and is almost incapable of walking. Pliny [col. 410] book 10, ch. 39: Those called apodes fly most of all, because they lack the use of their feet; by others they are called cypseli, of the swallow kind. Also: They have no rest except in the nest. They either hang or lie. Others too write the same. Moreover, since the cypselus is a sea bird, or a bird of the riverbanks, why should it be said to nest in the dry places of Idumaea? Mercerus urges in vain that the word cypselus is not far from the Hebrew קפוז kippoz. For that counts for little when the other marks are lacking. Not to mention that a word plainly of Greek origin is wrongly derived from the Hebrew language. For cypseli are so called ἀπὸ τῶν κυψελίδων [apo tōn kypselidōn], from the little cells which they build for themselves out of mud. The Philosopher, History, book 9, ch. 30: Οἱ δὲ ἄποδες, οὓς καλοῦσί τινες κυψέλους, νεοττεύουσιν ἐν κυψελίσιν ἐν πυλοῦ πεπλασμένας μακραῖς [Hoi de apodes, hous kalousi tines kypselous, neotteuousin en kypselisin en pylou peplasmenas makrais]. So in Herodotus, in Terpsichore, the son of Eëtion is given the name Cypselus, ἀπὸ τῆς κυψέλης [apo tēs kypselēs], in which he had lain hidden and escaped the danger of death.

The third interpretation, which explains קפוז kippoz as the blackbird, has more probability. 1. For blackbird in Greek is κόσσυφος [kossyphos], which could seem to have been formed from the Hebrew kipphoz, as the ancients pronounced it, by a metathesis of letters. 2. And it seems it can be reckoned among the solitary animals, since Varro ^{b)}, Festus ^{c)} and Isidore ^{d)} would have merula [blackbird] so called because it flies mera (that is, alone). 3. The same bird could rightly be called קפוז kippoz from leaping, since it hops rather than walks. Pliny book 10, ch. 38: Some birds walk, like crows; some hop, like sparrows and blackbirds. These were Junius's reasons for rendering kippoz as blackbird. But that most learned man did not consider that the Prophet is there dealing with φιλερήμοις [philerēmois] animals, desert-loving ones, by whose habitation a place formerly cultivated becomes waste and dreadful. No one would say the blackbird is of that number: it is a harmless bird, comely in form, sweet of voice, pleasant in taste, its dung most useful for enriching fields, so much so that Varro book 3, On Agriculture, ch. 5, wants it kept in aviaries together with nightingales. They do indeed say it is called merula because it usually wanders alone and does not usually associate with birds of its own kind except for the sake of its brood. But this derivation, along with others of Varro's, is ridiculed by Quintilian book 1, ch. 5: Who, he says, would not be pardoned after Varro? who wanted to persuade Cicero (for he writes to him) that ager [field] was so called because something agitur [is done] in it, and graculi [jackdaws] because they fly gregatim [in flocks]; although it is manifest that the one comes from the Greek, the other from the cries of the birds. But it was worth so much to him to make the turn, that merula, because it flies alone, was named as if mera volans [flying alone] [III, 197]. And indeed that merula is said as if merivola is pure invention; yet merula could have been said for mera, that is, alone, as a diminutive. But wherever it got its name, there is no one who does not know that it lives in inhabited places, and that one species of blackbird mostly frequents ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων [epi tōn keramōn], upon the tiles of roofs, as the Philosopher observes in History, book 9, chapter 19. Hence some refer here that saying of the Psalmist: I was like a solitary sparrow upon the roof.
